entries.title: The Best Automatic Litter Box of 2026: Petkit and Litter-Robot
entries.summary: With these high-tech automatic litter boxes, gone are the days of scooping and smells. Welcome to the future.
entries.content:
Featured in this article

I can confidently say that having an automatic litter box has been the biggest game changer for me when it comes to cat ownership. I can't recommend them enough. They can be pricey, but never having to scoop poop again is priceless.

We at WIRED—well, our WIRED cats—tested a dozen of the highest-rated and most technologically advanced automatic litter boxes on the market for at least a week, often more (using standard clay clumping litter unless otherwise indicated), to see if they were really worth the money—or the hype. Our new favorite automatic litter box is the Purobot Max Pro 2 because of its compact design and camera for monitoring. The Litter-Robot 4 is a close second, mostly because of its LitterHopper attachment that easily refills litter for you. Plus, we still love the more basic Petkit PuraMax 2 (and think it's a great option for most people).

Check out our related guides, like the Best Automatic Feeders, Best Cat Water Fountains, Best Pet Cameras, and Best Cat Toys. More of a dog person? We've got you covered; see our Best Dog Accessories.

Updated September 2026: We've added the PetPivot AutoScooper 12 and Whisker Litter-Robot EVO, and updated links and prices throughout.

Others We Tested

PetPivot AutoScooper 12 for $200: This is a good automatic litter box for this super-low price point, and if your budget is $200, this is so much better than a traditional box. However, I still think the picks above are the cream of the crop. This is the new-and-improved version of the 11 model below. It doesn’t have a connected app, which I don't love because I like to track my cat’s weight and usage, and I like being able to adjust settings from afar. But if you’re looking for a more hands-off model without much maintenance, a simpler, budget box like this may be a good option. Setup was super easy—all you need to do is put the included waste bags in the bin, attach the top, pop on the feet and ramp, and fill the litter. It’s on an automated timer and starts cleaning about four minutes after it senses the cat has left, but you can also do a manual cleaning and litter leveling through the buttons on the outside of the machine. PetPivot claims that it can hold waste for up to 10 days without needing to empty, but I found that the bottom waste drawer (which is less enclosed than other models I’ve tested) started smelling like wet sewage after a few days and needed more frequent emptying. There’s also no option to set different times for cleaning after usage, and often small litter clumps from urine would stick to the grate because it didn’t have enough time to solidify. There’s also no option to completely empty the litter in settings, which made it difficult (and messy) when I wanted to deep clean and when donating. My main gripe is that my cats kicked out so much litter during use due to the low, open-top design. If you go with this model, be sure to use litter tracking mats or have a vacuum cleaner on standby.

PetPiviot Autoscooper 11 for $170: This automatic litter box doesn’t have all the bells and whistles of some others on this list, but if you’re looking for a basic, inexpensive automatic box, I’d recommend this one. It has an open-top design that remains fully open throughout the cleaning cycle and has sensors to know when the cat has used the box and when or if the cat reenters during the cleaning cycle. Like most others, it spins dirty litter from clean using grates, and the dirty litter is deposited in a drawer below the box. The litter box is the smallest and lightest I’ve tested, and the only assembly required was popping on the legs and inserting the drawer (and putting a waste bag liner in). There’s no app required for use, and functions can be controlled by three buttons on the box—clean, refill litter, and power on/off. When you want to completely empty the litter, you attach a plastic cover that pops on to scoot all of the litter into the drawer below. Since this has no app, you won’t be able to closely monitor your cats’ usage or get alerted when the drawer is full, so this requires more check-ins than other WIRED-tested automatic boxes on this list.

Whisker Litter-Robot 5 Pro for $899: This model is part of Whisker's newest Litter-Robot lineup, which also includes the mid-level Litter-Robot 5 and the base-level EVO. It has an AI-enabled camera that can recognize up to five cats and WasteID technology to determine what type of visit your cat had—the only model I've tested with this capability. The dual-camera system captures external motion outside the box and inside the litter bed. It also charts trends over time to help you more accurately understand your cats' health and habits, so you know if anything is amiss. Plus, depending on the type of waste, LR5 Pro gives more targeted odor control, cycling immediately for solid waste and waiting for urine to make sure it clumps. The drawer is also more sealed and larger, with up to 10 days of waste storage per cat. It looks similar to my personal favorite auto box, the Litter-Robot 4 (above), but has a built-in camera, a touchscreen rather than physical buttons, a wider and shallower drawer, and a taller (removable) lip in the entryway. Maybe I'm just partial to the older model, but I think all of these changes make it less user-friendly than the 4 model. The touchscreen is finicky, the drawer liners are harder to place perfectly with the shallow design, and the removable entryway lip is much harder to attach and detach with smaller insertion tabs that feel like they could break off. Setup took several days because onboarding requires scanning a QR code with the built-in camera, but the camera never auto-captured the code. It'd be much easier if you could enter the code manually rather than relying on the camera. The camera always panned to the outside of the box rather than inside, and rarely showed footage of the stool/pee. Plus, the AI to differentiate cats only works reliably with the Whisker+ paid subscription plan ($80/year).

Petkit Purobot Ultra for $800: I liked this automatic box a lot, even if some of the features are a little over the top. (Read the full review here.) It uses a camera and AI technology to monitor litter box usage and lets you see your cat’s stool to help you more closely monitor their health. This upgrade has a large horizontal footprint and a camera on an arm in front of the opening, which swivels and follows your cat when it senses motion and records inside the litter box (it also has night vision). It has auto-bagging and -sealing features, so you never have to deal with the stool. The app logs and monitors usage, including the number of times used and the average duration. The camera has 180-degree viewing, two-way audio, and 24/7 streaming. It uses AI to identify which cat used the box, and while it doesn’t explicitly note whether a cat peed or pooped, you can review the footage to determine. Although this is a good idea in theory, the videos inside the litter box aren’t hi-def and are always in black-and-white, which makes it very difficult to actually observe anything in detail. The arm’s placement is awkward, making it extremely challenging to refill the litter box. This litter box always worked well and kept smells at bay, but the AI analytics fell a little flat for me, and it was needlessly tough to refill the litter.

Litter-Robot 5 for $799: The middle model Litter-Robot 5 offers several improvements and design tweaks over the base Litter-Robot 4: easier assembly and waste removal; an LCD screen; and, if you have a Whisker+ subscription, a new WasteID feature that is supposed to distinguish between feces and urine. This only worked intermittently in the first four months of testing, as did the LR’s ability to tell my cats apart by their weights. However, the firmware on the 5 was recently updated and has improved greatly over time, with fewer error codes and more consistent WasteID readings. I very much prefer Litter-Robot’s larger opening to Petkit’s, the ease of cleaning, and the fact it can hold 10 days' worth of waste from my two cats before needing to be emptied. It's also a step up from the base-level EVO in that it can accommodate five cats up to 30 pounds. I highly recommend adding on Litter-Robot's new ramp ($75) and litter-trap mat ($50), either of which helps to cut down on litter tracking, but both together resulted in a significant reduction in how often I had to vacuum. —Kat Merck

Petcove PurrTek Covered Self-Cleaning Litter Box for $360: I was surprised when my two large cats easily took to this very small automatic litter box. I wasn’t even sure my 16-pound cat would be able to fit inside. Set up was super easy: Just insert the step (my cats preferred to use it without because they’re so large and it took up valuable real estate inside), plug in, download the connected app, and connect the box to Wi-Fi. The waste bag was already installed, and there were also large buttons on the front to manually control settings like auto- or manual-cleaning, deodorization, auto-leveling, waste or litter emptying, and sensing. I’ve grown to really appreciate easy outside buttons, which are a game-changer when the often buggy app crashes or you aren’t near your phone. Like many automatic litter boxes I test, this product would be vastly improved with a better app interface and clearer English translations. It was very hard to figure out what the settings were asking or even if they were set, mostly because of the poor translation. Waste bin calibration could be set from zero to 15, and litter leveling setting could be set from zero to six, seemingly arbitrary numbers that didn’t seem to change settings. “Do not disturb” mode could be set, but only for a specific clock time, such as 11:30 pm, rather than a time span, which wasn't useful. It also took an egregiously long time to sift the waste, at almost four and a half minutes for the whole cycle. I wish the waste bin were at the bottom of the device, because emptying and refilling the bag was often messy and had litter leakage. The device worked without issue overall, and my cats liked it, but for almost $400, I’d get the Petkit PuraMax 2, which fluctuates at a similar price but works so much better.

Els Pet Orbitie for $300: This is one of the least expensive automatic litter boxes, but it functions much like the more expensive models, with an internal 65-liter-capacity orb that rotates and catches clumps with a plastic grate, depositing them into a bag-lined box below. The opening is a generous 12 by 12 inches—plenty big enough for my two 8-year-old cats, who took to it almost immediately despite never having seen anything but a traditional litter box. The accompanying Orbitie app doesn’t offer an extensive amount of information; it tells the user the volume of litter and what step of the cleaning phase the box is currently in, as well as how many times the box has been used and at what times. The first test unit I received was faulty—it sent multiple phantom alerts to the app, letting me know it had cleaned itself as many as 36 times a day, which I knew for a fact was not true. The replacement unit, however, works just as intended, though the bin beneath fills up fast (about every other day with my two cats), and it needs to be disassembled and cleaned every month or so, as tiny pieces of cat litter have a tendency to get in the gears beneath the orb and make a loud grinding noise. Online reviews panned an earlier version of this box, but Orbitie says this is an improved version. Thankfully, like the bigger brands, Orbitie also offers a 90-day money-back guarantee if you’re on the fence. —Kat Merck

FurryTail Automatic Litter Box Pro for $250: I was surprised by how quickly and easily my cats took to this device—even my larger cat, who hates change, started using it right away. Setup was super easy, and the box comes with a year's supply of waste bag liners, an additional grate attachment, and a mat to reduce litter tracking. Similar to many models, the spherical orb rotates, sifting dirty litter into a waste bag, which, on this model, is on top of the machine rather than below. The box has both a manual display and buttons on the machine, as well as an app to adjust settings. I'd include this model in our top picks because of how easy it was to set up and use, as well as how much my cats liked it, but the app was basically useless. Through the app, you can adjust settings like timed cleanings and do-not-disturb modes, manually clean, and monitor waste levels. However, the app never tracked usage or weight, and for the majority of the time, didn't clean when I manually instructed it to. The sensors would sense ghost cats and refuse to clean, with the device not automatically cycling for the majority of the day (which sort of defeats the purpose). This automatic box has tons of potential, but I can't fully recommend it until the kinks (especially in the app) are ironed out.

Casa Leo Leo's Loo Too Automatic Litter Box for $650: This automatic litter box was a top pick for a long time, but it's pricey and a bit cramped for some cats. We still like it, but think the options above are better for most people (and cats). There are four weight sensors inside the barrel to detect when a cat is still inside (it needs just 1 pound of weight to detect your cat), an anti-pinch sensor (for fingers and paws), and a radar system that detects when anyone, feline or human, is near it. For extra cleanliness, it also uses ultraviolet light for extra sanitation. The Smarty Pear app alerts you when the drawer is full (about once a week), records the times your cat uses it and the cat's weight, and you can set it to automatically clean six seconds to 20 minutes after your cat uses it. You can start a cleaning session manually from the app or use your voice if you connect the box to Alexa or Google Assistant. Former WIRED reviewer Medea Giordano’s biggest struggle using the Loo Too was pouring new litter into it, which can be tricky because of the small entry hole. The barrel is also pretty cramped, especially for her 12-pound cat.

PetSafe ScoopFree SmartSpin Self-Cleaning Litter Box for $350: This basic automatic litter box is around half the price but has a similar design to more expensive models. This futuristic-looking pod on legs has a rubbery bottom, a weight detector that sets off the cleaning cycle a few minutes after your cat has done its business, and a slide-out tray in the bottom. After they’ve been, the body rotates, and a mesh catches the clumps and deposits them in the tray, where there’s a bag with a wee deodorizer unit that smells like watermelon. You can connect it to Wi-Fi and review your cat’s toilet visits in the app on your phone, where each entry displays the time they went, their weight, and toilet trip duration. This self-cleaning box was easy to build and works surprisingly well, even though it feels kinda cheap. Ultimately, as a relatively affordable self-cleaning device, the PetSafe ScoopFree SmartSpin is worth a look. —Simon Hill

Not Recommended

Petlibro Luma Smart Litter Box for $600: I'm a big fan of Petlibro's automatic feeders and fountains, but I've found that the brand's other tech products, like this automatic litter box and AI-enabled pet camera, aren't on the same level. First, we cannot recommend any model that closes completely during cleaning cycles. The Luma is outfitted with tons of sensors to prevent cleaning while a cat (or any object) is inside or near the entrance, and I highly doubt injury would occur. But the globe spins backward and forward, rather than clockwise and counterclockwise, meaning that the entrance is closed during cycling. If a sensing malfunction happened, the cat would be trapped inside. I appreciated the button controls on the outside top, which allow for manual control. However, they're on a touchscreen above the camera. So, oftentimes, when I tried to manually reset, the camera caught me and wouldn't continue the cleaning or control I asked of it, because the safety features would prevent action inside the box. It was very frustrating. When I went out of town, it got stuck in the middle of the cleaning cycle for two days because it kept sensing a ghost cat. The globe was mid-cycle, and the entrance was covered; I couldn't bypass via the app to keep cleaning. (Thank God I had a second litter box for my cats available, or I would've been out of luck.) The auto-deodorizing feature goes off automatically for five minutes after each use and sounds like an airplane engine. There's no way to turn it off; you can turn the power down to a lower level, but it's still egregiously loud. Right now, I can't recommend this model (mostly for safety reasons), but a lot of the design flaws could be fixed in future iterations to make it a solid choice.

Oneisall Ease S1 Self-Cleaning Litter Box for $230: Full disclosure: I tested this in a beta version before it was released to the public, so I hope my major complaints have been fixed in later manufactured models. This automatic box is constructed from hygienic stainless steel to keep things cleaner and less prone to harboring odors, it has a simple design, and it’s affordable. I’m generally a fan of Oneisall’s pet tech; I’ve been impressed by various models of the brand's simple, affordable automatic pet fountains and automatic pet feeders. This model is also super simple, with a few front-facing buttons to control settings and no connected app. On the front is the status light, which will flash different colors for things like waste basket full, improper installation, and motion detection. It has buttons for turning off manual or auto-cleaning modes and leveling litter. For the first five days of “testing,” the automatic box detected a cat and stayed perpetually in cleaning mode. No matter what buttons I pressed, there was no way to override or reset it; even when I unplugged and replugged, the cleaning cycle would continue without end. When leveling litter, it would sense a ghost cat and stay perpetually in a wonky position for hours, if not days. Once it eventually went into standby mode, the litter wasn’t flat, and the box was slightly angled. My cats were too freaked out to use it regularly because it was always moving or at an odd angle. I love that it’s affordable, simple, and has hygienic stainless-steel construction, but some serious design changes need to be made—primarily a way to override ghost sensing to complete a cleaning cycle, and perhaps a connected app—before I can recommend this model.

PetSnowy Snow+ Self-Cleaning Litter Box for $530: This box looks like something from Kubrick’s visions of space travel, or if Eames started making plastic litter boxes. It takes up quite a bit of horizontal floor space, so it may not be ideal for those in cramped apartments looking to conserve space. Unlike all others on this list, this globe is closed during cleaning, which could cause injury if the machine malfunctioned and didn’t sense a cat. The box also doesn’t tell you when the litter’s low or needs to be refilled. My cats had a really hard time using it—they just couldn’t understand that it was a litter box. Older cats could have a tough time jumping into it, and the smaller opening could be a problem if you have bigger cats. It might be great for someone who wants to keep things tidy—it’s extremely clean, smells good, and hugely reduces litter tracking. However, we just can't recommend the device since it's closed during cleaning, which is not safe.

The Pet Zone Smart Scoop for $166: This is probably the least “smart” automatic litter box we've tested—it's a typical rectangular plastic box with an automatic arm that acts as a rake and scoops the clumped (soiled) litter into a small bin on the other side. Once the cat leaves, it begins a 15-minute countdown and the rake slides over the length of the box, (ideally) scooping up the waste and lifting it into the receptacle. You’re only allowed to fill the device with about an inch and a half of litter, which my cats didn’t like (they prefer a few inches to really bury it). The rake doesn’t stop when it's in the cleaning cycle—even if something jumps in, which is potentially dangerous. My cats tend to pee on the side of the litter box, which, because of the rake’s placement, means it misses an inch on either side—I still had to scrape the caked-on litter from the edges. The cycle timing can’t be adjusted, so the litter didn’t have time to clump completely, and the rake would immediately break it down into smaller clumps that would then be missed because they were too small. For me, the hassle's not worth it, and I’d rather just scoop it myself.

How Do Automatic Litter Boxes Work?

Automatic litter boxes vary depending on the brand and litter type. Generally, they have sensors, either by motion or weight, to tell when a cat has entered or exited the device. Usually customizable and controlled via app on your phone, or on a more rudimentary timer system, the cleaning cycle will begin a short time after the cat has used the box. With dome-shaped litter boxes, the cleaning will happen via a cycle where the litter spins and rotates around the spherical interior; the bigger soiled clumps will be deposited into the waste basket while the clean granules pass through the grates and get recycled back into the box.

The Petkit PuraMax 2, for example, rotates backward and then forward (rather than a clock-wise/counter-clockwise spin cycle) to sift the clumps from the clean litter, depositing the larger clumps into the waste basket. The Pet Zone Smart Scoop is the most rudimentary design we tested, simply using a rake attachment to scoop the bigger clumps into a waste receptacle in the back.

Are Automatic Litter Boxes Safe?

Pet owners should always do research and make an informed decision regarding which box is best for them and their cat. We only tested automatic litter boxes that remain open during cycling to ensure that if for some reason the weight sensors didn't pick up on a cat being inside, the cat could jump out. We don’t recommend devices that close completely because of the potential that the machine could not sense the cat and kill it during its automatic cycle.

These automatic boxes use sensors—some only needing 1 pound of weight to detect your cat—where the cycle will automatically stop no matter where it is in the cleaning process. Many also have anti-pinch sensors. For added security, the devices on this list have customizable schedules, including “do not disturb” modes. If you're a neurotic helicopter cat mom like me, you could only run the clean cycles when you choose, like when you're in the room to observe the cycle (although if you do that, the box won't stay clean for as long).

Where Should I Put the Automatic Litter Box?

All of these automatic litter boxes require electricity, so they will need to be near an outlet. Since cats will generally take a little while to get comfortable with their new potty, I recommend that you keep your old litter box until they use the device regularly. It helps to put the new automatic litter box near the old boxes to familiarize your cat with it. Adding in litter attractant and using old litter from the previous box also encourages your cat to use the new model.

As a general rule, for old-school litter boxes, you should have one box for each cat, plus one. With automatic models constantly cleaning, there is less need for multiple options, but we recommend leaving your old litter box out for an extended period to ensure the cat has acclimated to the new automatic box.

What Should You Look for When Shopping?

After testing around a dozen automatic litter boxes, I look for several things that make day-to-day life with the device easier for you and your pet. First, the connected app. This is what you'll be checking daily, so it's important that it works well. This is one of the reasons the Litter-Robot 4 was our top pick for a long time: its connected app is intuitive, simple to use, and reliable. I absolutely love the Petkit models we've tested, but the app is subpar, overcrowded with ads for other products and poorly translated. I also look for anything that makes filling litter easier: I love the Litter-Hopper attachment, which refills litter for you on Litter-Robot models, the self-filling litter reservoir on Homerunpet, and the self-sealing waste bags of the newest Petkit models. You'll also want to keep the cat's size in mind. My two cats are large, so I tend to opt for something with an extra-large, front-facing hole. Which box you choose depends on litter type and compatibility—if you're using tofu litter, make sure you get a model that is compatible with your preferred type. Budget is also a factor, with some models as low as $150 or as high as nearly a grand.

How Does WIRED Select Models to Be Reviewed?

I do a lot of research, looking up other reviews online, including our competitors, to see which are getting buzz. Since I'm the pet tech writer here at WIRED, I also have knowledge from other pet tech brands I love for things like automatic feeders and pet water fountains. Most of these brands also have automatic litter boxes, which I always try to test among their lineup of new pet tech. I also talk to other cat-parents to see what they're using (and liking). I aim to test a wide range of styles and price points for every type of budget and cat.

How Does WIRED Acquire the Boxes?

Sometimes we reach out to brands we're excited about and receive samples for potential review; other times we will buy a model we're interested in and expense it.

What Does WIRED Do With Them After Testing?

We keep some models on hand for long-term testing to see if they hold up over time. This is especially useful for our former top pick, the Litter-Robot 4, whose Litter-Hopper attachment eventually stopped working, or the Petkit models, whose AI starts falling flat without a Care+ subscription. Keeping some devices for longer-term testing helps ensure that we are giving our readers a comprehensive review. Most boxes we test for several weeks and donate locally upon completion.

History of the Automatic Litter Box

Rudimentary automatic litter boxes have been around since the late ’80s. These early models featured an automatic rake attachment (much like the Pet Zone Smart Scoop box) but had problems with reliability and loudness. It wasn’t until the 2010s that the devices started incorporating advanced tech like Wi-Fi and app control. In the decade since, that technology has continuously grown and improved, with most devices providing insight into your cats’ habits and health—truly becoming an asset in understanding your feline friends even better.

What I'm Testing Next

My cats are currently testing the Petkit Purobot Max 3, the newest model in beloved brand Petkit's automatic litter box lineup; and the Bissell CleanWell Self Cleaning Litter Box, the first automatic litter box model in the cleaning titan's new pet tech category.

entries.content:

The fee varies depending on the description or length of the video, ranging anywhere from $30 to $200, and if a guy wants her to say his name, “that is going to cost more because it’s not resalable,” she says from her home office in Orlando. “They want me to come on to them, to say that I’ve noticed them staring at me. That type of thing.”

But this request was a first for White. He “wanted me to be his mommy and tell him how he came out of my body, as he’s fucking me. It was just really awkward,” she says. White, who has 11 grandchildren and eight great-grandchildren, declined the request but says that sort of thing comes with the job when you are a septuagenarian sex worker.

“I am so surprised, but younger guys really want to be with older women,” she says.

Outside the Instagram-polished demographic typically associated with creators on OnlyFans and Fansly, where youth is among your most marketable assets, there is a growing demand for a different kind of digital seductress: the GILF.

Older creators have flooded adult platforms in recent years as demand for mature content has skyrocketed. On Pornhub, searches for “GILF” increased 129 percent in 2025, and “maturing MILF” was among the platform’s leading trends, according to figures the company shared with WIRED. In the US, the market for silver foxes was even more explicit: last year the top relative search term in Oregon was “horny grandma” while Maine’s was “granny sex.”

In the evenings after she’s finished sifting through messages, White turns to camming. “My shows,” she calls them. In one stream the night following the midterm elections, she dressed up in a silk-and-lace maid outfit, imploring fans to “cum and catch the action.”

White first entered the business at 65, following a decades-long career as an accountant, working with the Score Group, an adult media company in Miami that runs dozens of porn sites, including 60plusmilfs.com. She mostly works as an “independent contractor” these days, uploading content between Streamates, LoyalFans, OnlyFans, and her personal website. In all, White pulls in around $12,000 a month with the help of her daughters, who coordinate her social media posts and help make any necessary artwork.

Aging performers like Rita Daniels, 76, and Aunt Ann, a 69-year-old footwear model whose turnoffs include “mean people, liars, [and] limp dicks,” have found big audiences as the desire for GILF content grows.

Two of Aunt Ann’s explicit videos showing penetration have over 600,000 views on Pornhub. Others creators, like 66-year-old Monika Weiss, are “finally exploring every delicious desire I kept hidden for far too long,” as she writes in her OF bio. The genre has gotten so widespread across the industry that, in August, ASN—the adult entertainment company that hosts an annual awards ceremony—added a category for GILF of the Year.

White initially got into porn because it was “something fun to do” with her husband (they were swingers, and he would often post videos of their group trysts online). But after a series of unexpected financial setbacks—the family’s manufacturing business, which her daughters took over, started to suffer as the economy worsened—she realized porn was a smart alternative to help boost her retirement savings.

“It was a combination of things going bad. I realized that the retirement wasn't going to be there like I expected,” she says. “I would need to have more than just that social security check.”

Despite its challenges, platform-dependent work has provided older adults new opportunities at a second or even third career. “Some workers were pushed into the gig economy, with unemployment or forced retirement compelling them to seek out new financial lifelines,” says Brooke Duffy, who researches the intersection of social media and labor at Cornell University. Against this backdrop, she adds, “OnlyFans offered not only a stopgap but also a potential pathway through which to wrest back control over the conditions of work” by broadening the pool of participants through a new funding model.

Older women aren’t the only creators benefiting from a resurgent interest in mature porn. When Rick Kelson was let go from his contract position at NASA in 2021, where he worked as an engineer, sex work became his main source of income, “essentially a full-time job,” he tells WIRED. It was during this period that “the market for more mature performers, daddy types, was really starting to take off,” and a friend who’d worked with various gay film studios, “thought I had exactly the look that they wanted,” Kelson says.

Broad-shouldered with a thick white beard, Kelson, who turns 60 next year, believes the industry has finally caught up to mature porn because studios realize that it isn’t the niche genre they previously wrote it off as. “The mainstream traditional studios weren’t interested in playing to that market. As far as making content available, it just didn't seem like a profitable option before. They didn’t realize how large it was.”

Kelson averages $4,000 to $5,000 a month posting between OnlyFans, JustForFans, Pornhub, and RawFuckClub, on top of personal training and masseuse work. But despite the steady stream of income he has been able to build for himself, he acknowledges how difficult it is to make a living wage in this line of work “unless you are really, really hustling and pushing some boundaries, doing some of the real hard legwork.”

Today, more than a quarter of adults over 50 rely on side hustles to survive, according to a 2023 AARP survey, with 44 percent of older workers saying they have experienced a “job disruption” since 2018.

Octogenarian actress Donna Mills joined OnlyFans this year. In October, the former soap star told ABC News that though she has yet to post x-rated content, she wasn’t completely ruling it out in the future. “Provocative, maybe. I’ve always been a bit spicy.” Mills told ABC that she won’t honor fan requests for videos of her brushing her teeth but noted that she planned to fulfill one specific request: “stomping grapes.”

“I think it’s sexier to be not just totally naked … and have a little imagination about it,” she said of her approach.

White, who has 40,000 Instagram followers, says what’s happening right now has a lot to do with new attitudes around aging and who gets to monetize their image online. “I realized that the generations are changing. They’re not stifling sex like they used to. That way of thinking is so different from when I was younger, and a lot of women have benefited from that.”

Even so, Kelson believes the volatility of the job market will continue to push older adults to subscription platforms to supplement their income. “More of them will see that they have that option,” he says. Mostly, he’s been ecstatic to see creators in his age bracket get into the business.

“I love it because it pushes back against the concept that as you get older, you have to lose pieces of your life that you enjoy,” he says. “We are not freaks just because we have a high libido at the age of 65 or 70 or whatever.”

entries.title: Kitchen Composters I Recommend After 2 Years of Testing (2026)
entries.summary: After enduring years of smells, strange noises, and waste “tea,” I’ve found the composters and food recyclers I’d actually recommend.
entries.content:
The countertop kitchen composter is a lovely thought. Instead of a smelly bucket of vegetable scraps and coffee grounds breeding fruit flies on your counter or attracting rats to your backyard, you could just put it all into a nifty electric gadget. Then, at some undetermined point in the future, you'll have a bountiful supply of nutrient-rich compost to use in your garden.

Unfortunately, none of the more popular electric kitchen composters do exactly this. Though some of these devices are marketed as “composters” and include instruction booklets and companion apps detailing the many ways to use compost, most will only grind up and dry your food scraps. You will greatly reduce your food waste output, and it will no longer smell, but if you’re hoping to put eggshells and banana peels into a machine and magically scoop out the kind of compost you’d buy at the garden center, that’s just not going to happen.

That said, you can mix small amounts of these grounds into potting soil in tiny ratios or use them as a feeder for a “real” compost pile. But again, most of these machines are meant for reducing the volume of household food waste. This is, itself, a legitimate goal, as cast-off food makes up an estimated 24 percent of municipal solid waste, resulting in the release of methane, a destructive greenhouse gas, as it breaks down in the landfill.

Or maybe you'd just like your food grounds to be odor-free and shelf-stable before adding them to your green waste bin for municipal composting or your backyard compost. In any case, despite critics’ cries of greenwashing and corporate astroturfing, there is indeed value to these devices. They make people more aware of their food waste. They don't use a huge amount of power (around 1 kilowatt-hour was typical in my testing). And my top pick, the Reencle Essential (8/10, WIRED Recommends), even produces something close to compost.

Also, be sure to check out our guides to the Best Indoor Gardening Systems and Best Smart Bird Feeders.

Updated November 2026: I’ve added Reencle's new Essential model as my new top pick, and ensured up-to-date links and prices.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

Featured Products

Best Overall

As I mentioned above, none of these machines makes truly ready-to-use, biologically stable, fully decomposed compost, but Reencle comes closest to creating what you'd scoop out of a traditional compost bin or pile. Popular in South Korea years before it appeared in the US, Reencle machines arrive with a starter bag of Reencle Compost Starter (which you can purchase separately for $52) containing activated carbon, wood pellets, glucose, and a trio of patented thermophilic microbes ready to chow down. There's also a prefilled charcoal filter that slots into the back.

The Essential is Reencle’s newest—and least expensive—model, with a refreshed, contemporary exterior; controls on the front instead of the top; and a lid that opens and closes manually. It's too large for a kitchen counter, but it conveniently operates much like a heated trash can. The lid opens via a manual button on the top of the unit, and in goes your organic matter. That's it. There are no cycles, tablets, or auxiliary buckets to worry about, and the cycle is barely louder than a refrigerator fan—about 28 decibels. Within hours to days, depending on the item, the scraps break down into a material resembling a cross between dirt and sawdust.

The smell isn't always pleasant, but you can usually mitigate this with the control panel's Dry and Purify buttons or by adding what, in composting lexicon, is called “browns”—dry, carbon-rich materials, like bread or shredded paper. The Reencle also tends not to stink when you feed it its preferred diet of 1.5 to 2.2 pounds of scraps per day. Unlike other machines, it can also accept meat and dairy.

When the volume reaches the fill line, it’s time to scoop out the grounds. At this point, you can mix the grounds with potting soil at a 1:4 ratio and leave it to cure for three weeks. (I used a large tub in my garage for this step.) Afterward, you can use it for both outdoor and indoor plants. I’ve used the resultant mix to positive effect both indoors and outdoors.

Dimensions 13.3 × 12 × 17.2 inches
Capacity: Minimum 1.5 pounds, maximum 2.2 pounds
Can't process: Large bones or shells, fruit pits
Cut food into small pieces before adding? Yes
Fastest waste breakdown: 2 to 24 hours or longer, depending on the items
How to use its output: Sift, mix 1:4 ratio with soil, cure for three weeks, and add to plants indoors or outdoors; add to compost pile
Warranty: 2 years

Also Great

The Prime is Reencle’s original flagship model. It's pretty much identical to the new Essential, but with the controls on the top instead of on the front, plus a convenient sensor-activated auto-open and -close lid. The entire top also hinges open, making it easier to scoop out the grounds for curing. It's only about an inch taller than the Essential but accepts the same 2.2 pounds of kitchen scraps per day.

I found its fan noise to be slightly less intrusive than the Essential above, despite both units measuring at 28 decibels. It’s ultimately up to you if this, plus the auto-close lid, feels worthy of spending an extra $100. (I did like the latter feature very much.)

Also worth noting is that one of the stirring paddles broke off my Prime after a year and a half of daily use. I contacted Reencle to ask what customers should do in this situation. I learned that if the Reencle is within the warranty period (two years for units purchased on or after May 13, 2026; one year for units purchased previously), they can contact customer service to receive a paddle repair kit at no charge. If the unit is outside the warranty period, a kit runs $35. I don't love that this has happened, but Reencle's models remain the best of these devices available, and I've found the company's customer service to be responsive and easy to work with.

If you need a larger capacity: For larger households, there's also the Reencle Gravity ($649), which is Reencle's largest unit by both dimensions and capacity. It can accept 3.3 pounds of waste a day and sports the same convenient sensor-activated lid as the Prime. When I tested it last year, I found it to be significantly quieter than both the Prime and the Essential—not that either is noticeably loud, but the Gravity is nearly silent. I did, however, find that over time, the Gravity contents went anaerobic (read: smelly) much faster than with the Prime. The increased volume seemed to retain more moisture. If you go with a Gravity, I recommend keeping plenty of browns (old bread, shredded paper) on hand to maintain microbial balance or adding in a few more sessions of manual stirring per day with the included shovel.

Dimensions 12 x 13 x 18.4 inches
Capacity: Maximum 2.2 pounds
Can't process: Large bones or shells, fruit pits
Cut food into small pieces before adding? Yes
Fastest waste breakdown: 2 to 24 hours or longer, depending on the items
How to use its output: Sift, mix 1:4 ratio with soil, cure for three weeks, and add to plants indoors or outdoors; add to compost pile
Warranty: 2 years

Best Grind-and-Dry Food Recycler

Most kitchen “composters" simply grind and dry your food scraps, but the Lomi 3 countertop composter does the best job of this of the bunch. I'm always impressed when companies listen to feedback and adapt, and Lomi's most updated model solves a couple of the quirks found on the now-discontinued Lomi 2: Gone are the multiple modes, the annoying twist-off lid, and the need to put scraps right into the machine. Now there's a convenient 3-liter, 7.5-inch-tall countertop bucket, just like the FoodCycler below; an easy push-button lid; and Grow and Express modes. The Lomi 3 is also smaller and supposedly quieter than the Lomi 2, but my decibel meter found the difference to be negligible. One feature I did like on Lomi 2 that's missing from the 3, however, is Lomi mode, which could break down a list of approved bioplastics, including Lomi's own packaging. Lomi confirms the new model cannot accept bioplastics.

Like with the Lomi 2, there's a companion app for basic management, but I enjoyed not having to use it; simply press an on-device button, and the Lomi starts. When it's done (cycle lengths vary from three to 16 hours, depending on the amount and moisture level of its contents), it will play a little chime, and you can either put the processed grounds—which are very fine and look like Folgers—in your outdoor compost pile, top-dress your lawn with them, or add them to soil at a 1:10 ratio (1:15 if using meat or dairy). I also like that the Lomi 3 has a clear lid, so you can see exactly where it is in its cycle.

It's a lot to pay for what's essentially a grinder-and-dryer, which is why I generally recommend the Reencle above, especially if you want to generate something close to compost. However, for those simply looking to reduce their waste output, or who live in an area that's subject to composting fines, the Lomi 3 is a thoughtfully engineered, easy-to-use option.

Note that my test unit originally came with a lid that warped after several months, allowing odors to escape and attracting fruit flies. Lomi said the initial batch of lids was made with faulty plastic and sent a new lid, but the new version is starting to warp as well after a couple of months.

Dimensions 11 x 11 x 12 inches
Capacity: 3 liters
Can't process: High-sugar products, hard bones, hard shells, sawdust, unpopped popcorn, compostable plastics
Cut food into small pieces before adding? No
Fastest waste breakdown: 3 to 16 hours
How to use its output: Mix with soil at 1:10 ratio, or 1:15 if using meat or dairy; add to compost; sprinkle on your lawn
Warranty: 1 year (two additional years of LomiCare are available as an add-on for $140)

Another Great Grind-and-Dry Recycler

First off, I appreciate that FoodCycler doesn’t even pretend it's making compost. “The FoodCycler is a food-waste recycler,” the company explained firmly before agreeing to ship a test unit. “Our primary goal is to provide a modern food-waste solution for users who may lack access to traditional composting or other disposal options that divert from the landfill. Therefore, the resulting byproduct cannot be labeled as ‘compost.’” And indeed, the FoodCycler breaks down food so quickly, and with no microbial involvement, that there’s no way anyone could think this was actual finished compost. But if you are opting for a grinder/dryer, know that the Eco 3 makes more groaning and creaking noises while in operation than the Lomi 3 above, but it is still a great pick.

Launched in 2024, the Eco 3 is a smaller version of the Vitamix FoodCycler FC-50 (7/10 WIRED Recommends), sporting a larger 3.5-liter capacity and, according to FoodCycler, better grinding capability. At 11 by 9 by 13 inches, it is small enough to sit on a counter or tabletop, though the real convenience with this machine is its auxiliary pail. Fill the sleek, 8-inch-tall lidded container with scraps (in my household of three people, this took about three days). Once it's full, swap out the lids, seat it in the machine, and press a button.

A few hours later, you'll have a handful of “Foodilizer,” a "homemade soil amendment” that looks like finely ground dirt, per FoodCycler. The output is among the most finely ground of any of these machines. There's no assembly (other than filling a filter with carbon granules), no app, no making an account, no pods or tablets or choosing various cycles—you don't even have to plug it in until you're ready to use it.

The cycle runs from four to nine hours, depending on the water content of the scraps. Though its base sound is an audible but unobtrusive whir (about 36 dB on my decibel meter), it has started making loud groaning and creaking sounds after six months of regular use, so I only run it at night or when I won't be home. I also occasionally had trouble getting the bucket to seat correctly, but the manual addresses this, and I figured it out after a couple of tries.

Note: If you know you like the FoodCycler, but you need a larger capacity, FoodCycler's XL Eco 5 model (see Also Tried, below) can accommodate 5 liters of kitchen waste with slightly larger dimensions (14 by 14 by 10 inches). WIRED reviewer Nena Farrell tested the Eco 5 during the holiday party season, but felt the required space made the smaller Eco 3 a better grind-and-dry processor.

Dimensions: 11 x 9 x 13 inches
Capacity: 3.5 liters
Can't process: Compostable plastics, beef bones, candy, oils/fats
Cut food into small pieces before adding? No
Fastest waste breakdown: 4 to 9 hours
How to use its output: Mix with soil at 1:10 ratio, or 1:15 if using meat/dairy; add to compost; sprinkle on your lawn
Warranty: 3 years

A Decent Budget Grind-and-Dry Option

Like many of these devices, the R800 is called a “composter,” but it does not compost, and this detail irks me. There's a “Bio Compost” mode where you can add Airthereal Revive Magic Compost Starter. This is not included, costs $30 on Airthereal's website, and simply adds thermophilic bacteria, akin to the Reencle above. This will get the process started, but the result will not yield anything close to fully decomposed compost. To even achieve pre-compost, you will still need to mix small amounts with large amounts of soil and then let it cure for weeks.

However, amid the landscape of grind-and-dry kitchen-scrap processors, the Airthereal isn't half bad for the price. It's not as seamless or slick as the Lomi or FoodCycler, but it will effectively reduce the volume of your kitchen scraps. There's also a digital screen on the front that tells you what's happening. I also like that you can see into the machine thanks to its clear lid.

The biggest detractor was the lack of a lid for the bucket. The bucket is intended to sit in the machine (where there’s no need for a lid), but after using these kinds of devices for more than two years, I've found it is much more convenient to have a bucket handy for scraps while you're working, instead of having to periodically go over to the machine and press a button with dirty hands. Airthereal does make a bucket-and-lid option for an extra $60.

The R800 isn’t obnoxiously loud during its grind cycle, at about 40 decibels, and while there is an app, it's not required to use the machine. The device requires a fairly large footprint, so don't expect to put it on your kitchen counter. Another note: Remember that the carbon filter is on the back and its location is not immediately obvious—you will need to remove it and its stickers before using the device, lest you run the risk of going on an errand and coming back to the house smelling like a dumpster in the hot sun. (Don't ask me how I know.) Some Amazon reviews mention issues with overheating and jamming, but I've been using the Airthereal off and on for a year and have never experienced any mechanical issues.

Dimensions: 14 x 12 x 14 inches
Capacity: 5 liters
Can't process: Compostable plastics, beef bones, candy, oils, or fats
Cut food into small pieces before adding? No
Fastest waste breakdown: 5 to 15 hours
How to use its output: Not stated, but I recommend mixing with soil at 1:10 ratio, or 1:15 if using meat or dairy; add to compost; sprinkle on your lawn
Warranty: 1 year

Largest Capacity

All of these machines do a great job breaking down food scraps in some way or another, but none fully address what to do with them, absent a yard or compost pile. Adding them at a 1:10 (or even 1:15!) ratio to potting soil is kind of a pain, and many people don't have the space to store all this dirt. The Mill is the only device that solves this issue by allowing users to ship their grounds in a box via USPS to a farm in Washington state that repurposes the broken-down scraps for chicken feed (for an extra fee).

When I first tested the Mill in 2024 (6/10 WIRED Recommends), I didn't care for this idea, which seemed inefficient at best and canceled out the benefit of recycling the food waste at worst. I also didn't love the coarse texture of the grounds, having tried to use them in my garden and finding them too easily rehydrated. The price also seemed over the top for what's essentially an oversized Lomi. But if you're looking to reduce the amount of food waste leaving your house, the Mill has the best ease of use, requiring the least amount of work on a user's part.

Like the Reencle, it acts as a big trash can—you can throw in whatever you'd like at any time, and you can program a cycle any time you'd like via the app, which is exceedingly complete and user-friendly. There's an almost encyclopedic directory of what can and can't go in the machine, as well as a tracker that shows how many pounds of waste you've diverted over time. The Mill also has a massive capacity that only needs emptying about once a month—a claim I found to be accurate during my testing period. It's on the louder side at around 60 dB, so I highly recommend scheduling its processing cycle to run at night.

There are now two versions of the Mill: the Plus, which is the 27-inch version with a stylish wood-veneer top and lid-opening foot pedal that I tested, and the Essential, which is $200 cheaper, 4 inches shorter, and lacks the convenient foot pedal and wood-veneer finish. Both models have the same capacity.

Dimensions: 27 x 16 x 15 inches (Plus)
Capacity: 6.5 liters, or 40 pounds
Can't process: Large bones or shells, large amounts of oil or sugar/candy, compostable plastics/packaging, moldy meat
Cut food into small pieces before adding? No
Fastest waste breakdown: 3 hours to up to 24 hours
How to use its output: Send in provided boxes to a farm, add to your own compost, feed to your chickens, add to soil at a ratio of 8 cups per 10 square feet
Warranty: 2 years, 2 additional years available for $199

The Analog OG

In order to understand the intended purpose of electric composters, one first needs to know about the original indoor home composting method: the bokashi bin. Unlike traditional outdoor composting, which is straightforward anaerobic decomposition, the bokashi method, invented in Japan in the 1980s, is anaerobic fermentation. This method is a bit like quick-pickling your food waste to prep it for the decomposition process. The food scraps still need to decompose, but this gets it part of the way there with the least amount of hassle and time. In fact, some gardeners even prefer bokashi to compost, as the output retains nitrogen, a critical plant nutrient.

To start, put your food scraps in the included bucket, and once you have about a 1-inch layer of waste, add a sprinkling of microbe-infused bran (a 2-pound bag of bran with a little spouted measuring cup is included with the Bokashi Living kit). The instruction booklet for my Bokashi Bin also recommended putting a plate inside the bucket to push down the contents. Compost “tea,” or liquid byproduct of the fermentation process, can drain through a spigot on the bottom every couple of days and then be added to your outdoor plants. The smell is reminiscent of kombucha brewed in a hot dumpster with diapers and stale beer, so be sure to rinse out the cup each time.

Once your bin is full, let it sit for two weeks, and your food waste will have broken down enough to bury in your garden or add to your backyard compost. I admit I struggled with this part—after two weeks, my scraps looked much the same, only stinkier and slimier. Bokashi Living says on its website that this is normal: If it has a pickle-like smell and produces bokashi tea, it's a success.

I’ll admit it was refreshing at first to have a device that didn’t make noise, need maintenance, or use electricity, but a few weeks into testing the Bokashi Bin, I found myself sorely missing my Reencle. I didn’t keep a separate scrap bin on the countertop, so every time I needed to add refuse to the bucket, I had to peel the lid off with my dirty hands and remove the plate, which then made my hands even dirtier. The smell of fermenting food waste would then immediately—and as time went on, almost violently—permeate the kitchen and its vicinity. I certainly prefer any of the electric options listed above, but bokashi has its devoted adherents. If what I've detailed above doesn't sound bothersome to you, it may be worth a try.

Dimensions: 12 x 12 x 16 inches (approx.)
Capacity: 5 gallons
Can't process: Large amounts of liquids, fat, grease, large bones or pits, excessively moldy food
Cut food into small pieces before adding? Yes
Fastest waste breakdown: 2 weeks
How to use its output: Bury in your garden or add to backyard compost
Warranty: 1 year

Compare Our Top 7 Kitchen Composters and Food Recyclers

Composter Type Fits on Counter? Pros Cons Capacity
Reencle Essential ($349) Microbiaal No Comes closest to producing actual compost. Quiet and simple to operate. Push-button lid not as convenient as other Reencle’s sensors 14 liters
Reencle Prime ($449) Microbial No Comes closest to producing actual compost. Convenient sensor-activated lid. Stirring paddles may break off over time 14 liters
Lomi 3 ($449) Grind-and-Dry Yes Best grind-and-dry performance. Convenient lidded scrap bucket. Bucket lid may warp. Can no longer process compostable plastics. 3 liters
FoodCycler Eco 3 ($400) Grind-and-Dry Yes Produces extra-fine grounds. Convenient lidded scrap bucket. May develop creaking noises over time. Bucket is finicky to seat in the machine. 3.5 liters
Airthereal Revive R800 ($250) Grind-and-Dry Maybe Affordable. Large capacity for a grind-and-dry machine. No included scrap bucket. Less polished than competitors. 5 liters
Mill Food Recycler ($999) Grind-and-Dry No Optional mail-in program for the output. Well-engineered and easy to use. Very large and very pricey. Mail-in program is an add-on for price and carbon 6.5 liters
Bokashi Living Bokashi Bin ($83) Anaerobic fermentation Yes Silent and uses no electricity. Very affordable. Messy, hands-on process. Output is kind of gross. 5 gallons

Other Kitchen Composters I Tried

Clear Drop Organics Collector (OC) for $399: From the makers of the innovative Soft Plastic Compactor, this simple white box does not claim to grind, process, or compost your food scraps; it simply stores up to 3.5 gallons' worth of them in an enclosed container with a fan and carbon filter for odor control. For its part, the OC did this well. I also appreciated the included paper-bag liners, which made it easy to drop off the scraps at a nearby collection bin, as my town does not have municipal compost. I also loved the sensor-activated lid that slides back and forth. Clear Drop posits that municipal composting is the best option overall for reducing waste via compost, because the process can be standardized for quality and is easy for everyone to comply. I agree, but let's be real: You can get a carbon-filter compost canister for less than $30. If taking the compost out every couple of days instead of every seven days is a chore you're willing to pay $400 to avoid, then knock yourself out. But you should know that the OC makes a loud fan noise—40 decibels on my decibel meter—which annoyed everyone in my household so much that I didn't even make it through the full test period.

Vego Countertop Kitchen Composter for $360: This grind-and-dry processor is roughly the same size as the Lomi, with many of the same operational features, but it is significantly less expensive. However, there are definitely some inconveniences that come with the lower price point. For one, you need to add scraps into the bucket while it’s seated in the machine. You can remove the bucket, but unlike with the FoodCycler, there's no separate lid for the bucket, and the metal mechanism underneath is exposed. Further, the machine’s lid is a bona fide pain to get on and off, requiring precise alignment of notches and two hands to wrench it open or closed. Needless to say, this is no easy feat with fists full of scraps. Vego claims its Vego mode does create a biologically active soil amendment when processed with one of the included VegoTabs (packet of 30, $30 if purchased separately). In all modes, but Vego mode especially, the barrel turns every couple of minutes, emitting a loud whirring. Because the sound isn't constant, it's more noticeable. Even from 10 feet away, I found it obtrusive enough to want to turn up the TV volume.

GEME Terra II for $700: Billed as the first “AI-powered kitchen appliance that uses industrial-grade microbes to turn waste into living soil,” this machine was the largest and bulkiest one I've tested (12 inches long, 22 inches high) and operates much like the Reencle, with a heated, enclosed container and a bag of proprietary starter microbes. Instead of a replaceable carbon filter, it uses a metal-ion purification system. Also similar to the Reencle, the GEME does not make ready-to-use compost but, rather, pre-compost that can be mixed with dirt. The role AI plays in this process is unclear: I couldn’t find an explanation on the website, on the machine itself, or in the instruction booklet. (GEME says it is working on an improved description.) The Terra II's signature feature is that its industrial-grade microbes can withstand the supposed high heat of the breakdown process. However, when I put a temperature probe into the Terra II's pre-compost after I'd had it running for about a week, it was 97 degrees Fahrenheit—nowhere near hot enough to kill pathogens. Further, during my testing period, this machine emitted a constant fan noise, like a range hood on medium speed—46 decibels on my decibel meter, which was loud enough to be disruptive.

FoodCycler Eco 5 for $500: Like the Eco 3 above, this is a food recycler and doesn’t claim to create true compost. It’s a large, quiet machine; my 3-year-old likes to turn it on when I’m not looking, and I don’t notice until I see that the blue light is on. The result doesn’t look like compost, but it does get ground down to some bare-bones food bits after several extra cycles my son initiates with his sneaky button-pushing. Each cycle runs between four and nine hours. It hasn’t been stinky, and I’ve found it handy to have nearby in the kitchen for food waste. It is quite large, though—nearly as bulky as my robot vacuum station due to its 5-liter capacity. The cheaper Eco 3 is likely a more efficient use of space in the kitchen, unless you have a ton of food scraps on a regular basis and really need the larger-capacity bin. —Nena Farrell

How I Tested

I cook daily for my family of three, and I've been processing our kitchen scraps in these composters in my home kitchen since the summer of 2024. I tested each machine under typical household use for a minimum of four weeks each, and in several cases, six weeks or longer. I tested all cycles offered, with all manner of foods allowed, according to each manual. I even attempted to use the finished product in my yard and potted plants (to varying effect). I acquired the units either by purchasing them myself or receiving them as samples from companies (with no expectation of coverage). When I completed testing, I donated or returned some units and kept others in office storage.

Featured in this article

If you’re shopping for a unique gift idea this holiday season, these subscription boxes for kids are something young ones of all ages will get to enjoy not just on Christmas morning, but all year long. It can be something you know they’ll love, or just never-ending toys if it’s one of those ages where their interests are changing by the minute.

We’ve had all kinds of kid and parent testing with this guide. I’m the parent of a 4-year-old, while former WIRED senior editor Adrienne So tested kids subscription boxes with an 8-year-old and 10-year-old. Our latest recommendations were tested with a baby. Really, there’s no limit on what age these boxes can delight and teach. After years of testing, these are our favorites.

Looking for more kid gear? Don’t miss our guides to the Best STEM Toys, Best Baby Gear, and Best Kid Backpacks. Shopping for a parent? We’ve got gift guides for moms, dads, and new parents alike.

Updated November 2026: We’ve rearranged our top picks and updated our notes about Kiwi Crate and Lovevery’s subscription boxes. We also updated pricing information for all of our recommendations.

More Kid Subscriptions and Gift Boxes We’ve Loved

Keke Pouch Subscription for $40: Kids are small factories of chaos. The constant stream of worksheets, drawings, and crafts is great for encouraging creativity and hand-eye coordination, but every surface in our house is perpetually cluttered. Rather than contributing to the mess, the Keke (Keep Every Kid Engaged) bag keeps every item organized. This frankly adorable, durable, handled bag has four activities in separate pouches that clip into binder rings, and extra storage pockets for masks or hand sanitizer. Every 12 weeks, the Keke subscription sends three new activities in new pouches to swap out. (You need to buy the bag separately.) Even though the activities are aimed at 3- to 6-year-olds (and some, like a simple puzzle, were too easy even when my son was 5), I love these bags for travel. I’ve been experimenting with different travel organizers to hold all my kids' markers, stickers, and card games for travel, and the Keke Bag is the best I’ve seen yet. —Adrienne So

Lingo STEM Subscription Box for $40: Lingo was founded by Aisha Bowe, a former NASA scientist, and is intended to bring STEM skills to children who may have been underexposed. That description does not precisely apply to my 7-year-old, but he nevertheless enjoyed this kit. We tried In the Driver's Seat ($75), which teaches you how to build a backup sensor for a car. Mileage will vary, and the kit is technically aged for sixth to 12th graders. However, my son and I found it easy to follow along once we figured out how to log in to the Lingo portal and access all the videos on his iPad. We followed the video instructions in the portal to learn how to build circuits on a breadboard using lights and resistors, and program to turn the lights on and off. I particularly like that it doesn't purport to teach children coding via puzzle pieces or blocks but uses an actual circuit board and a real programming environment. Lingo also offers teacher support if you get stuck. However, I should note that while the kit contains all the hardware components you need to build the sensor, you will need your own iPad or laptop to access the videos and instructions. —Adrienne So

Literati Gift Book Box for $63: If you and your family are struggling to find reading material for your required 20 minutes of reading per day for school (that's not Wings of Fire over and over again), I highly recommend a book subscription. We paid for a Literati subscription until its curation system worked against them. Literati offers book clubs that take newborn children up to their teens. Literati will send your child five books each month. Return any books you don't like and pay Amazon's list price for the rest. Every book was a hit, and each kid had to have every book in every box. For the sake of my wallet and our already-groaning bookshelves, I had to stop the subscription. You can gift a subscription or a one-time, age-appropriate theme box with a card, personalized stickers, and artwork. It's a great way to expose your children (and yourself!) to wonderful new works of art or literature without dragging them to a bookstore. —Adrienne So

Sketchbox Monthly Basic Box for $25: Art supplies—drawing, painting, pastels—are the delight of my family's life. SketchBox is a monthly box, and each month has a theme that's put together by an artist. My daughter's charcoal box was assembled by mixed media artist Nikoli Shaver and included a graphite starter kit, a small pack of media-appropriate paper, an eraser, charcoal pencils, and more. This box has an amazing value—the Nitram starter kit alone costs $16, and my 10-year-old spent several days sketching, tapping, and blending. If you're unsure of where to start with watercolor or oil pastels and find wandering Blick's aisles intimidating, these boxes are a great place to start. You can get a basic box for $25 or a premium one for $35, which has a higher-quality selection plus a piece of art to inspire you. —Adrienne So

Stickii Club Sticker Subscription for $12: My kids' appetite for stickers is endless. I find them constantly, on the mirrors in our house, on their school planners and water bottles, and occasionally stuck to the back of my chair or in the car. Stickers are also an accessible way of supporting independent artists. Maybe you can't buy a painting or a T-shirt, but a sticker only costs a few dollars and you can display it everywhere. For $12 a month, Stickii Club offers three different sticker styles—Cute, Vintage, or Pop—along with a storage sleeve and three stationery items, like a notepad, card, or stamp. The club works with independent artists and illustrators (no AI-generated art yet) to produce sheets of original designs. We tried the Pop subscription. These stickers are marvelous. There's a huge variety in the sheets sent. Some are vinyl, some are transparent, but all are high quality and intricately detailed. The artist is also noted on each corner so we can look them up ourselves. My kids were delighted and traded them with each other like currency. I am now investing in Stickii folios (from $18) in the hopes that I can keep these just a little bit more organized (and sticking a few on my laptop while I'm at it). —Adrienne So

The Weekly Junior for $49: This has been a pretty news-heavy few years. Other parents may disagree with me, but my kids really want to know what's going on in the world around us—in a safe, understandable, kid-friendly way, of course. The Week Junior is aimed at 8- to 14-year-olds, and my 10-year-old can now read it herself. Every week, we cuddle on the couch while they look at pictures and pick out which current events to read about, like the Olympics, or whether apps should have likes. It's a great way to keep my kids informed without worrying that they'll hear swear words in my podcasts. —Adrienne So

entries.title: Can a Radar-Equipped AC Actually Cut Your Power Bill?
entries.summary: Air conditioners can now follow you from room to room to cut power draw. Saving the planet, however, won’t come from a smarter breeze.
entries.content:
With rolling heat waves sweeping the globe, 2027 is shaping up to be the hottest year on record. As the health risks of extreme temperatures mount, there's never been a better time to rethink sustainable cooling.

Air conditioners and electric fans account for around 20 percent of electricity used in buildings worldwide—3 to 4 percent of total greenhouse gas emissions—and, as demand for cooling in homes, workplaces, and schools grows, the number of AC units in use could reach 5.5 billion by 2050.

The solution isn't one magic fix, but a suite of emerging technologies heading for living rooms and apartment windows. From radar sensors tracking your body to compact heat pumps and climate-safe refrigerants, here is how the next generation of air-conditioning plans to keep us cool without cooking the planet.

The “Intelligent AC” Boom

In 1994, Mitsubishi Electric was zooming past the air-con competition, introducing the first motion and occupancy sensors for AC, with infrared 3D sensing eventually following in the mid-2010s. Fast-forward to 2026 and AI-powered ACs now track people in the home with millimeter-level precision.

AC makers have launched intelligent, targeted air conditioner units all year, from Samsung’s Bespoke AI system in March to Dyson’s Find+Follow feature for its Purifier Cool fan in June. At IFA in September, we got a whole sweep from Chinese companies like Hisense, Dreo, and Midea.

LG’s latest DualCool AI AC has a 5-meter radar sensor for people detection plus targeting based on your everyday movement patterns. Hisense’s Companion Living AC also uses data from smart home sensors to identify and precool “target paths” within the home, based on your routines. So if you always head from the couch to the kitchen for a midnight snack, your AC can cool that particular zone before you even get up.

The real-time cooling features aim to improve comfort inside sticky homes. A secondary benefit is that precisely locating people and delivering cooling directly to them could reduce energy consumption. “It definitely has the potential to reduce the total energy use for air-conditioning,” says Björn Palm, senior professor in energy technology at the KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm. By how much? That's less clear.

Dyson’s Find+Follow purifier and fan uses a simple, low-resolution camera, feeding the “stick figure”-like, anonymous coordinates of its 17-point person detection into an algorithm, all instantly processed on-device and deleted, without any face recognition. “It can tell that you’re a human, whether you’re sitting or standing, which direction you’re moving," says Alex Hudson, an environmental care engineer at Dyson. "It might map your arms and shoulders.”

The Purifier Cool can oscillate 350 degrees between “up to six people” in the space, directing airflow for personalized cooling. One hour after it detects that everyone has left the room, the appliance will switch to Auto mode and—if there is no big pollution spike for the purifier to deal with, like a truck driving past an open window—it’s a "considerably lower power draw than when it’s in fan mode, so there’s definitely a benefit there,” Hudson says.

Samsung’s Bespoke AI WindFree Pro adds a motion radar sensor, which can recognize and track two occupants. “AI Direct Wind” can follow and blast you for immediate cooling, whereas “AI Indirect Wind,” you guessed it, cools the spot you’re in without blowing air right in your face. Samsung’s residential environment tests claim energy savings of “up to 30 percent” with its overall AI energy mode switched on. At IFA, Samsung added wearable data: a Galaxy Watch or Galaxy Ring can signal to the AC when you’ve fallen asleep, triggering a gentler Windfree Cooling mode overnight.

Midea’s VitaBreeze AC, launching in early 2027, combines user photos with millimeter-wave radar sensors to personalize cooling. During setup, the user manually uploads a series of room images to the app, indicating the air conditioner placement. The AC then uses those images with radar data to create a 3D virtual grid of the room and furniture position.

Millimeter wave (or mmWave) radar—the kind used in 5G cellular technology—bounces short-wavelength radio waves, typically 1 to 10 millimeters, to detect an object's distance and angle, as well as tiny movements in real time. Here, the Midea app’s Follow Me feature, similar to Samsung's, can pinpoint your real-time position in the room, triggering louver adjustments as you move around. Manuel Seethaler, head of Midea's Residential Air Conditioning product strategy in Europe, says that its technology can save more than 30 percent of energy in cooling mode compared with units without these algorithms.

The average AC sold in 2024 was already about 20 percent more efficient than an equivalent model in 2014. However, there’s still plenty of room to grow, as the IEA predicts that “cooling demand” will grow by 1,600 terawatt-hours by 2035—Japan and South Korea’s total electricity combined. But this kind of proximity sensing could also result in marginal energy savings.

“There is a performance improvement you can get if [targeted AC] is done well,” says Vincent Romanin, founder and CTO of San Francisco–based Gradient, which makes 120-volt all-weather window AC/heat pumps. “But we’re going into buildings where we’re reducing the energy by 85 percent and to design another feature that gets us to 87 percent? I personally have never used a product with an occupancy sensor that I feel like worked well.”

Compact Window ACs

For Palm, to reach sustainable home cooling by 2050, we need three major changes: cheaper, compact heat pumps for all home sizes; fewer toxic natural refrigerants (fluids and chemical compounds that absorb and release heat); and newly designed systems with low charge to ensure safety.

Heat pumps have become a modern, efficient option for heating and cooling. For heating, it's a four-stage process: absorbing outside heat to produce gas via a refrigerant; compressing to raise the temperature; condensing, where heat is passed to the water in your home’s heating system; and cooling back into a liquid via an expansion valve to drop the pressure. When cooling is needed, the reversing valve switches back to run the process from inside to outside for air-conditioning.

The key is to persuade renters and people living in smaller homes to make the overall switch. “For the domestic market, we need heat pumps which fit into an apartment without being too noisy or bulky,” Palm says. It's also critical to reduce the price.

Gradient units typically use one-third less energy than a standard window AC, mostly for heating but with cooling efficiencies too. They’re a quick self-install option that lets apartment renters get their window back, see lower bills, and run a quieter AC system than older models.

But fixing the form factor only solves part of the equation. Palm’s other criteria—replacing toxic synthetic refrigerants with natural alternatives like propane (R290), as in Bosch's Climate 6000iP, which launched in September—present a tougher engineering challenge. Leaking refrigerants alone account for an estimated 720 million metric tons of CO2-equivalent emissions every year. Natural refrigerants dramatically curb the potential for global warming, but their flammability demands complex, spark-free redesigns and low-charge systems that US regulators and supply chains are still cautious about embracing.

Reaching sustainable cooling by 2050 won’t be glamorous, Palm says. Ultimately, the future of home cooling won't hinge on an air conditioner that tracks you to the kitchen for a midnight snack—it depends on the unsexy, invisible mechanical work happening deep inside the compressor.

entries.title: Greenlight Family Hub Digital Wall Calendar Black Friday Sale (2026)
entries.summary: The Greenlight Family Hub displays your family calendars, manages your kid’s chores, and doubles as a photo frame. It’s also already discounted ahead of Black Friday.
entries.content:
I've tried almost every digital wall calendar available (as is my job as WIRED's resident calendar tester), and the model that I've found increasingly impressive as time goes on is the Greenlight Hub.

Greenlight has a different premise than other digital wall calendars. The brand started as a debit card for kids before branching into more app-based categories: chores to attach to allowance distribution, family location tracking, and more. Greenlight launched its own Family Hub device to bring these features together and add a few more, like the digital calendar function, seen in popular tools like Skylight.

Now, Greenlight's Family Hub is at its best price, already on sale ahead of Black Friday. The 15.6-inch version I tested has a $100 discount, totaling $199 right now (significantly less than every other digital wall calendar I recommend, all of which usually retail for at least $300). There's also a smaller 10.1-inch model available for $30 off, currently selling for $169, if you want something a bit cheaper.

Meet Greenlight’s Hub

The Greenlight Hub leads with its family calendar tool that lets you see everyone's schedules in one place, but it also has tabs for chores, family locations, and even doubles as a digital photo frame at no extra cost. You'll have to subscribe to Greenlight's Family Hub+ plan to get family location sharing. That subscription also grants access to Greenlight's voice assistant, which allows you to ask the hub questions.

The Greenlight Family Hub is overall a great device, particularly for parents who want to track how well their kids complete chores. (Conveniently, you also have the option to attach an allowance, if you'd like.) I've been enjoying it just fine with a 4-year-old whose only chore is to brush his teeth at night.

But no matter whether you have kids, the Hub is a worthy addition to any home. I like the modern, stylish icons that feel cooler and more gender-neutral than the bubbly, pastel interface featured on the Skylight and similar tools. The Greenlight also doesn't share the decidedly Android feel of some cheaper models, despite being less expensive than those other options right now.

Ultimately, I'm impressed with how well the Hub performs as a digital photo frame, calendar, and even voice assistant. The sale is a big one—the perfect opportunity to get a handy, stylish digital wall calendar for your family ahead of the holidays, or perhaps a gift for your mom or another family you know would love it.
